What a 404 actually means, and why your site probably gets it wrong

Filed under: engineering, web infrastructure

Every developer has seen a 404. Fewer have thought carefully about what the status code is actually asserting. HTTP 404 Not Found is a statement about a resource, not about a page: the origin server is telling the client that it has no representation for the requested target, and that it is not going to speculate about why. That is a narrow, honest claim, and it is far more useful than the alternatives most content management systems reach for.

The trouble starts when a site decides that returning a 404 looks unfriendly. A designer adds a nicely illustrated page not found screen, someone wires it into the router, and somewhere along the way the status line quietly becomes 200 OK. The page still says the words page not found in large friendly letters, but every automated consumer of that URL now believes the request succeeded. Search crawlers index the error screen. Link checkers report the link as healthy. Monitoring dashboards show a perfect success rate while every single visitor lands on an apology.

Soft errors are worse than hard errors

The industry name for this is a soft 404, and it deserves the mild contempt the name carries. A hard error is loud: something upstream can react to it, retry it, alert on it, or fall back. A soft error is silent by construction, because it has deliberately disguised itself as a success. The information that would let a machine do the right thing has been discarded in exchange for a nicer looking screen, and the screen could have been just as nice with the correct status attached to it.

The same pathology shows up in maintenance pages. A deployment goes sideways, the platform swaps in a we will be back shortly banner, and it serves that banner with a 200 because the banner itself rendered fine. The correct answer is 503 Service Unavailable, ideally with a Retry-After header, and it costs nothing to send.

Bot walls have the same shape

Challenge pages are the third member of this family. If you have ever watched an interstitial that sits there checking your browser for a few seconds before letting you through, you have met one. The interstitial is doing something reasonable from the origin's point of view, but it is almost always served with a 200 status, and the body it returns has nothing to do with the content anybody asked for. An automated client that trusts the status code will happily parse the challenge screen as though it were the article, the product listing, or the API response it went looking for.

This matters enormously for anything that reads the web on your behalf. A scraper that stores a challenge page as though it were content will silently poison a dataset. A language model handed a challenge page as context will answer the question it was asked, confidently, from text that has no bearing on the question. The failure is not that the tool crashed. The failure is that it did not.

What to do instead

Send the right status code. Send 404 for a missing resource, 410 when you know the resource is gone for good, 503 during maintenance, and 429 when you are rate limiting. Put the friendly illustration in the body of the response where it belongs, alongside the correct status line rather than instead of it.

On the consuming side, assume the status line is necessary but not sufficient. Check the shape of what came back. A response of a few hundred characters whose first sentence is an apology is not the article you requested, whatever number preceded it. Anything that automates a judgement about web content should be able to refuse to make one.

None of this is difficult. It is simply unglamorous, which is why the 404 on your own site is quite possibly returning 200 as you read this.
